newsitem.title: USA: Angry Washington police want federal takeover.
newsitem.headline: Angry Washington police want federal takeover.

text.p: Demoralised by a wave of killings and their inability to stem the tide, Washington's police union is lobbying for a takeover of the force by the federal government, union leader Ron Robertson said on Friday.

"Our first desire is for the federal government to take over," he said. "We have no game plan (for fighting crime). I'm standing in the middle of a killing field. We are fighting a battle and we are losing the war."

Robertson, chairman of the Fraternal Order of Police, said he sent a letter to Democratic President Bill Clinton asking for the federal government to take over management of the police force and was lobbying Republican leaders in Congress.
The crisis in the police reflected deepening trouble for the nation's cash-strapped capital, which has already had its finances taken over by a federal control board.

Robertson said absorbing the city force's 3,300 members into the Justice Department would provide direct access to the facilities of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and other federal agencies, helping it to battle crime.
"It would also give us experienced management and a plan," he said.

While murder rates have been falling in other major U.S. cities, homicides in Washington are running at the same pace as last year when there were 399 slayings, up 10 percent over 1995. So far this year, police have reported 46 murders. The record was set in 1993 when 467 people were slain.

Washington police are outraged over the murder early on Wednesday of police officer Brian Gibson, 27, who was shot four times in the head, neck and shoulder while he sat in his patrol car idling at a traffic light. The alleged killer had just been ejected from a nearby nightclub.
Hundreds of police are planning to march as a sign of solidarity at Gibson's funeral in Washington on Monday.

Robertson said the Washington police department was so short of funds matters were becoming dangerous for police as well as citizens. The slain officer, for instance, was alone in his car when he was shot because Washington cannot afford to have two officers together on the night shift.

"We are losing 10 experienced officers a month (to retirement) and we have trouble recruiting replacements," Robertson said, citing a $27,900 annual starting salary. Neighbouring police departments in Maryland and Virginia pay beginning salaries of between $30,000 and $32,000.
"The starting salary in Los Angeles is $40,000," the union leader said. "Why are we worth so much less?"

He estimated it would take an infusion of about $700 million "to bring us up to speed" with other major city police departments with the money spent on salaries, overtime, equipment and programmes to combat crime.
"Someone has got to do something," he said. "Ninety juveniles were murdered here last year. Eighty-three were arrested for murder. It's nuts."

Washington police were able to make arrests in only four out of every 10 murders last year, well below the level in previous years. Police blame budget cuts and staff shortages as well as the random nature of the murders.
With the city close to bankruptcy, Clinton proposed to Congress in his latest budget plan a federal takeover of $3.9 billion worth of city programmes, including its prisons.
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, citing the crime rate, deteriorating schools and streets, urged Clinton to meet with congressional leaders on ways to help Washington solve its financial problems.
"We're sitting high and dry at the White House and Congress and there is deterioration all around us. It's unacceptable," the Mississippi Republican told reporters.

Asked if he thought the police should be federalised, Lott replied, "I think that drastic problems call sometimes for drastic action. I have to think about what that would mean in terms of dollar responsibility and the self-government that they have in the District of Columbia."
"But ... when you have a nation's capital that is not safe not only for people but for policemen, something has to be done. Something has to be done."
